title: Channel kinetics shape firing
objective: Predict how channel inactivation and potassium currents shape a neuron's firing pattern.

steps.title: Why some neurons adapt fast
steps.body:
A1 introduced RA and SA neurons. Part of the difference is the transduction channel itself. A channel that **inactivates quickly** under sustained force passes current only briefly, so the neuron reports change and then falls silent.

Piezo2 currents inactivate rapidly, which fits its role in many rapidly adapting touch neurons (A4).

flag.note: Adaptation also depends on ending structure (e.g. capsules around endings) and on K⁺ and Nav channels.

steps.title: K⁺ channels set the rhythm
steps.body:
Several K⁺ currents shape firing. Some activate slowly during a burst and progressively slow it (spike-frequency adaptation). Others set how quickly the neuron recovers between spikes.

Change the K⁺ channel mix and the same stimulus gives a different spike pattern.

steps.scenario: Two DRG neurons get the same 1-second current step in a patch-clamp recording.
steps.prompt: Which explanation best fits neuron A?
options: The neuron is unhealthy and dies partway through the current step
Strong K⁺ currents or fast Nav inactivation let it fire only at onset
It has no sodium channels at all, so it cannot sustain any firing
The injected current step was simply too small to drive more spikes
steps.explanation: Single-spike ('phasic') firing to a sustained step usually reflects intrinsic properties such as strong K⁺ currents or rapid Nav inactivation. Neuron B's slowing train is classic spike-frequency adaptation.
steps.followUp: Firing pattern under current injection is one of the fingerprints used to classify DRG neuron types in culture (C11).

steps.prompt: Myelin speeds conduction mainly because it…
options: It adds extra sodium channels evenly along the whole axon length
It insulates the axon so spikes jump between nodes, skipping most membrane
It makes the axon thinner, which on its own speeds the signal up
It prevents Nav inactivation, so the spike never needs to reset
steps.explanation: Saltatory conduction: myelin reduces leak and capacitance, so the signal hops from node to node. This is why myelinated Aβ fibers conduct far faster than unmyelinated C fibers (A5).

variants.setup: Compare a myelinated Aβ axon and an unmyelinated C axon.
variants.prompt: Which carries its spike faster, and why?
options: The C fiber, because it is thinner
The Aβ fiber, because myelin lets spikes jump node to node
Neither; they conduct at the same speed
The Aβ fiber, because it lacks sodium channels
variants.reveal: Myelin insulates the axon so the signal leaps between nodes (saltatory conduction) — far faster than continuous conduction in a bare C fiber. (Aβ axons are also thicker, which helps, but myelin is the main reason.)

steps.setup: A toxin slows Piezo2 inactivation, so its current lasts as long as the force does.
steps.prompt: What would you expect from a normally rapidly adapting touch neuron?
options: It stops responding to force entirely once inactivation is slowed
It fires for longer under sustained force, acting more slowly-adapting
It switches over to detecting heat instead of mechanical force
Nothing changes, since inactivation speed does not affect firing
steps.reveal: If the transduction current persists, the receptor potential persists, and so does firing. Channel kinetics translate directly into coding.

variants.prompt: A mutation makes Piezo2 inactivate much more slowly. A normally rapidly adapting touch neuron will now…
options: Stop responding to touch altogether
Keep firing during sustained force, more slowly-adapting
Start responding to heat instead of force
Fire in exactly the same way as before
variants.explanation: If the transduction current persists, so do the receptor potential and the firing — channel kinetics set how fast a neuron adapts.

reviewNotes: Confidence medium: adaptation mechanisms simplified (flagged). Textbook-level.
